title: Longest Palindromic Substring — Manacher's Algorithm
directAnswer: Find the longest substring that reads the same forwards and backwards. Expand-around-center is O(n²) and is the answer most candidates should reach. Manacher's algorithm gets it to O(n): transform the string by inserting separators so every palindrome is odd-length, then sweep left to right maintaining the rightmost palindrome [center, right]. Inside that boundary you seed each radius from its mirror before expanding, so each character is examined O(1) amortized times.

remember.pattern: Mirror reuse inside the rightmost palindrome boundary (like Z, for palindromes)
remember.formula:
transform: "#a#b#a#"  (n -> 2n+1, all palindromes odd)
p[i] = radius of palindrome centered at transformed index i
if i < right: p[i] = min(right - i, p[mirror])   mirror = 2*center - i
expand while chars match; if i + p[i] > right: center = i, right = i + p[i]
answer length = max(p[i]); original start = (i - p[i]) / 2
rules: Insert separators (`#`) between and around every character so even- and odd-length palindromes both become **odd** in the transformed string — one case to handle, not two.
`p[i]` in the transformed string equals the palindrome **length** in the original string (a neat consequence of the `#` padding).
Inside the current `[center, right]`, seed `p[i]` from its mirror `2*center − i`, **capped at `right − i`** — past `right` you haven't verified symmetry.
Only the explicit expansion can push `right` rightward, and `right` never retreats — that monotonicity is the O(n) proof, exactly as in the Z-algorithm.
Map back carefully: original start index is `(i − p[i]) / 2`. Off-by-one here is the most common Manacher bug.
whenToUse: Longest palindromic substring with a strict O(n) requirement
Counting all palindromic substrings in linear time
Queries about palindrome radii at every center
When expand-around-center's O(n²) is too slow for the input size
antiSignals: n is small or O(n²) is acceptable → expand-around-center is far simpler and less bug-prone
You need longest palindromic *subsequence* (non-contiguous) → that's DP, not Manacher
Only checking if the whole string is a palindrome → two pointers, O(n), no transform
Counting distinct palindromes → palindromic tree (Eertree), a different structure
remember.takeaway: Manacher is the Z-algorithm idea applied to palindromes: the `#`-transform removes the odd/even split, and a rightmost-palindrome window lets each new center borrow its mirror's radius before expanding. Reach for it only when O(n) is genuinely required.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can first give the clean O(n²) expand-around-center, then explain why naive checking is wasteful and how mirror symmetry inside a known palindrome removes the redundancy.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Botching the index mapping between the transformed and original strings, or forgetting the min(right − i, mirror) cap so symmetry is assumed past the verified boundary.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Lead with expand-around-center (the realistic interview answer), then derive Manacher's mirror trick and the right-never-moves-back invariant, and convert p[i] back to original coordinates correctly.

problemStatement:
Given a string `s`, return the **longest substring** of `s` that is a palindrome (reads identically forwards and backwards).

If several palindromes share the maximum length, returning any one of them is acceptable. A single character is a palindrome of length 1.
constraints: ASCII characters; the separator `#` must not appear in s (or use a sentinel not in the alphabet)
Return any one longest palindrome if there are ties
understanding: You're locating the widest mirror-symmetric contiguous block. The naive idea checks every substring; expand-around-center grows outward from each possible center; Manacher removes the remaining redundancy by reusing palindrome radii already discovered, via the symmetry inside the rightmost known palindrome. The `#`-transform is the trick that collapses the even/odd center cases into one.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Substring or subsequence?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Substring — contiguous. Longest palindromic subsequence is a separate DP problem.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I need O(n), or is O(n²) acceptable?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Decides the approach. Expand-around-center (O(n²)) is the expected default; reach for Manacher only when the input forces O(n).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are ties acceptable?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — return any longest palindrome. Track the first or last maximum, your choice.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I assume a separator character is available?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: For Manacher, yes — `#` works if it isn't in the alphabet; otherwise pick a byte outside the input's character set.

approaches.name: Expand Around Center
approaches.whenToMention: This is the realistic interview answer — give it confidently before mentioning Manacher. It's simple, correct, and usually fast enough.
hints: A palindrome is defined by its center. How many centers are there? n single-character centers (odd length) plus n−1 gaps between characters (even length) → 2n−1 centers.
From each center, expand two pointers outward while the characters match and stay in bounds. The widest expansion over all centers is the answer.
Track the best (start, length) seen. Each expansion is O(n) and there are O(n) centers → O(n²).
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are 2n−1 centers; each expansion can grow up to n/2 steps → O(n²) total. Only a few indices of bookkeeping → O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Expand-around-center grows palindromes outward from every possible middle.

**Centers, not substrings.** Every palindrome has a center: a single character for odd lengths, or the gap between two characters for even lengths. There are `n` odd centers and `n−1` even centers, `2n−1` in total — far fewer than the `n²` substrings the brute force checks.

**The expansion.** From a center, set a left pointer and a right pointer and move them outward while `s[left] == s[right]` and both stay in bounds. When they stop, `s[left+1..right−1]` is the maximal palindrome at that center. Compare its length to the best so far.

**Handling both parities.** Run the expansion twice per index `i`: once with `left = right = i` (odd-length palindrome centered on a character), once with `left = i, right = i+1` (even-length palindrome centered in the gap). Take the longer.

**Why it's the right default.** It's short, hard to get wrong, and `O(n²)` clears typical constraints (`n ≤ a few thousand`) comfortably. State it first; only escalate to Manacher when the interviewer pins the input size at something that needs linear time.
approaches.insight: The leap from O(n³) to O(n²) is realizing you don't enumerate substrings — you enumerate the 2n−1 centers and let each palindrome reveal its own length by expanding. Manacher's further leap is noticing that neighboring centers' expansions overlap, so many comparisons are redundant.

approaches.name: Manacher's Algorithm (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: Bring it out when O(n) is required. Frame it as 'the Z-algorithm trick for palindromes': transform to kill the even/odd split, then reuse mirror radii inside the rightmost palindrome.
hints: Even and odd palindromes are annoying because they have different center types. Insert a separator like '#' between every character and at both ends: "abba" → "#a#b#b#a#". Now every palindrome is odd-length and centered on a real position.
Define p[i] as the radius of the palindrome centered at transformed index i. Maintain the rightmost palindrome you've seen as [center, right].

If i is inside [center, right], its mirror j = 2*center − i already has a known radius. Seed p[i] = min(right − i, p[j]) — capped because beyond 'right' you haven't checked symmetry — then expand explicitly. If you pass 'right', move the window.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each explicit expansion step increases 'right', and 'right' only ever moves forward across the 2n+1 transformed positions. So the total expansion work is O(n). The mirror seeding is O(1) per index. Building the transformed string and mapping back are O(n). Total O(n) time, O(n) space for the transform and the p array.
approaches.explanation:
Manacher's algorithm computes, in linear time, the palindrome radius at every center by reusing symmetry the way the Z-algorithm reuses prefix matches.

**Step 1 — the transform removes the parity split.** Build `t` by inserting a separator `#` between every pair of characters and at both ends: `"abba"` becomes `"#a#b#b#a#"`. This has two effects. First, `t` always has odd length `2n+1`, so *every* palindrome in `t` is odd-length and centered on a single index — the even/odd case distinction disappears. Second, because of the padding, the radius `p[i]` of the palindrome centered at `t[i]` equals the *length* of the corresponding palindrome in the original string. That coincidence is what makes the bookkeeping clean.

**Step 2 — the rightmost-palindrome window.** Sweep `i` left to right over `t`, maintaining `center` and `right`, the center and right edge of the palindrome discovered so far that reaches farthest right (`right = center + p[center]`).

**Step 3 — borrow from the mirror.** When processing `i`, if `i < right`, then `i` lies inside the current palindrome, which is symmetric about `center`. Its mirror index is `j = 2*center − i`. By symmetry, the palindrome at `i` is at least as wide as the one at `j` — *up to the boundary*. So seed `p[i] = min(right − i, p[j])`. The `min` is essential: beyond `right` the characters were never compared, so you can't assume the mirror's full radius carries over. If `i >= right`, start with `p[i] = 0`.

**Step 4 — expand and slide.** After seeding, try to extend: while `t[i + p[i] + 1] == t[i − p[i] − 1]`, increment `p[i]`. These comparisons happen only past the current `right`. If the new palindrome reaches beyond `right`, update `center = i, right = i + p[i]`.

**Why it's linear.** Every successful character comparison advances `right`, and `right` moves only forward across `2n+1` positions. So across the entire sweep there are at most `O(n)` successful comparisons, plus one failing comparison per index. The mirror seeding is constant time. That's the whole `O(n)` argument — identical in spirit to the Z-algorithm's monotone `r`.

**Step 5 — map back.** The answer length is `max(p[i])`. The starting index in the original string for that center is `(i − p[i]) / 2`, because each original character sits at an odd transformed index and the `#` padding doubles positions. Slice the original string from there for `p[i]` characters.
approaches.insight: Manacher is Z-thinking for palindromes. The `#`-transform turns 'two kinds of palindrome' into 'one kind', and the rightmost-palindrome window lets each new center inherit its mirror's radius for free, paying real comparisons only when it extends past everything seen — which, because the boundary only moves forward, totals linear work. Use it only when O(n) is mandatory; otherwise expand-around-center is the saner choice.

code.python:
def longest_palindrome(s: str) -> str:
    if not s:
        return ""
    t = "#" + "#".join(s) + "#"
    m = len(t)
    p = [0] * m
    center = right = 0
    best_len = best_center = 0
    for i in range(m):
        if i < right:
            mirror = 2 * center - i
            p[i] = min(right - i, p[mirror])
        while (i - p[i] - 1 >= 0 and i + p[i] + 1 < m
               and t[i - p[i] - 1] == t[i + p[i] + 1]):
            p[i] += 1
        if i + p[i] > right:
            center, right = i, i + p[i]
        if p[i] > best_len:
            best_len, best_center = p[i], i
    start = (best_center - best_len) // 2
    return s[start:start + best_len]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(longest_palindrome("abba"))
    print(longest_palindrome("babad"))

Nested palindromes; mirror reuse seeds most radii, expansion stays O(n) overall.

commonMistakes: Reaching for Manacher when expand-around-center's O(n²) was acceptable — needless complexity.
Dropping the min(right − i, mirror) cap so symmetry is assumed beyond the verified region.
Mismapping transformed indices back to the original string (the (center − radius)/2 step).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the boundary cap on the mirror
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Beyond 'right' the characters were never compared. Copying the full mirror radius assumes symmetry you haven't verified and over-reports the palindrome length.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
if i < right:
    p[i] = p[2 * center - i]   # ignores the boundary
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if i < right:
    p[i] = min(right - i, p[2 * center - i])

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong index mapping back to the original
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Each original character sits at an odd transformed index. The start in the original string is (center − radius) // 2; using center − radius (without /2) slices the wrong substring.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: start = best_center - best_len      # transformed coordinates, wrong

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Using Manacher where expand-around-center suffices
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Manacher is intricate and easy to get subtly wrong under interview pressure. If O(n²) clears the constraints, the simpler center expansion is the safer, more communicable answer.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: # n <= 1000 but candidate writes full Manacher with index bugs
commonMistakesDetailed.good: # n <= 1000: expand-around-center, O(n^2), simple and correct

patternNote: Mirror-reuse within a rightmost boundary — the same engine as the Z-algorithm, specialized to palindromes via the #-transform. Recognise it for linear-time palindrome radius/length queries; otherwise expand-around-center is the pragmatic default.
